<description>
This sets `permissions: contents: read` on the CI workflow, which is all the jobs use.

On this repository the token is already read-only, through the repository's default. The workflow's `permissions` key then adjusts that default ([GitHub docs](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/workflow-syntax#how-permissions-are-calculated-for-a-workflow-job)), so the setting now lives in the workflow.

The same change for libsecp256k1 is bitcoin-core/secp256k1#1964.

Closes #36512.
</description>

[2026-10-14] r:5511616075 review COMMENTED by hebasto (member) (edited 2026-10-14):
I see this change as controversial.

While demoting the `packages` permission from `read` to `none` looks good in principle, it has no practical effect for this repository, as nothing in `ci.yml` pulls from GHCR.

Moreover, enforcing permissions on behalf of forks seems outside this project's scope.

[quoted text omitted]
It is [not dropped](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/actions/runs/38451588370/job/115483571315):
```
GITHUB_TOKEN Permissions
  Contents: read
  Metadata: read
```
[2026-10-14] c:6167704263 comment by fametrano (contributor):
You are right: `Metadata` is not dropped. The job log on the PR head lists `Contents: read` and `Metadata: read`. The master job lists `Packages: read` as well. So the change drops only `Packages`. Nothing in `ci.yml` uses it, so as you say it has no practical effect today.

On forks, I take your point: their token settings are for their owners. I have removed that claim from the description.

What remains is that the permission is written in the workflow, instead of only in the repository setting. If that is not worth two lines, I am fine with closing the PR.
</new_statements>
